main.title: Crusader of Centy
main.subtitle: A sword and an unfamiliar voice
main.summary: Crusader of Centy is Nextech's overhead action adventure, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 17 June 1994.

cards.heading: A sword and an unfamiliar voice
cards.text: Crusader of Centy is Nextech's overhead action adventure, first released for Mega Drive in Japan on 17 June 1994. Known as Soleil in Europe, it follows Corona, a boy who receives his father's sword when he turns fourteen. He begins exploring a world threatened by monsters, fighting directly with the sword and solving obstacles along the way. A change in his ability to communicate soon alters the journey: he loses the capacity to speak with people and gains the ability to understand animals and plants instead.

cards.heading: Travelling with animals
cards.text: Animals encountered during the adventure can become travelling companions, lending Corona abilities when equipped. His dog can restrain an enemy, while a penguin gives the sword an ice attack. Two abilities can be equipped at once, so choosing companions changes both fighting and access to the landscape. New powers create a gradual sense of growth without relying on conventional experience levels. The animal cast also makes exploration personal: another creature joining the group can provide a solution to a barrier the player has already noticed elsewhere.

cards.heading: Understanding the other side
cards.text: The story eventually restores Corona's ability to speak with people and takes him through time to investigate the conflict between monsters and humanity. Earlier assumptions acquire another meaning as he learns more about that history. Producer and writer Yayoi Onda designed the adventure around the gradual acquisition of skills, with the animal companions becoming central to its world. The result gives its approachable swordplay a changing perspective: progress comes from learning what others can do, then using that knowledge to reach places and understand events that were previously closed to him.

main.title: Pocky & Rocky 2
main.subtitle: Natsume · Super Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Pocky & Rocky 2 is Natsume's Super Nintendo action sequel, sending Pocky on another adventure through monsters and places drawn from Japanese folklore. She moves freely around stages viewed from above, throwing talismans at enemies and travelling with a supporting companion. A second player can take control of that companion, with different allies providing their own attacks and abilities. The sequel changes the balance of the partnership. Pocky remains the central traveller, while the person beside her becomes a changing set of useful possibilities.

cards.heading: A shrine maiden brings more company
cards.text: Pocky & Rocky 2 is Natsume's Super Nintendo action sequel, sending Pocky on another adventure through monsters and places drawn from Japanese folklore. She moves freely around stages viewed from above, throwing talismans at enemies and travelling with a supporting companion. A second player can take control of that companion, with different allies providing their own attacks and abilities. The sequel changes the balance of the partnership. Pocky remains the central traveller, while the person beside her becomes a changing set of useful possibilities.

cards.heading: The companion is part of the toolset
cards.text: Pocky can throw a partner toward an enemy for a powerful attack or temporarily take on the partner's abilities through magic. Choosing an ally therefore affects how an obstacle can be approached. In single-player, the computer handles the companion; a second player can instead provide direct assistance. The supporting role has unlimited lives, creating a different relationship from the equal vulnerability of the first game's two characters. The pair still share the scene, but the sequel gives their cooperation a more explicitly organised purpose.

cards.heading: A different way to share the screen
cards.text: Attack upgrades and protective clothing help Pocky survive the successive stages, while another companion can alter the rhythm of a familiar encounter. The visual world retains its animated creatures and folklore imagery, making the expanded cast feel at home beside her. Released in Japan in 1994, with overseas editions following, the sequel develops cooperation by giving the second character a distinct role. Its interest lies in what the partnership makes possible: the same central hero can answer a new situation differently because somebody else is travelling alongside her.

main.title: Robotrek
main.subtitle: Building a robot party
main.summary: On July 8, 1994 Enix released Slapstick in Japan, later localized in North America as Robotrek.

cards.heading: An inventor begins an adventure
cards.text: Enix released Slapstick in Japan on July 8, 1994, later localizing it in North America as Robotrek. Developed by Quintet with Ancient, the RPG gives its young inventor a laboratory's worth of possibilities: he creates robots, combines items and modifies equipment. The robots become his fighting party, while the invention system makes experimentation a regular part of the journey.

cards.heading: Building the party
cards.text: The protagonist builds up to three robots to fight on his behalf. Their equipment, special attacks, body colours and names can be customized. Program Points determine their attributes, while programmed sequences produce special attacks and other effects. Creating a useful party therefore involves deciding how each machine should be equipped and which actions it can perform.

cards.heading: Inventing and combining
cards.text: An invention machine lets the player create and combine items for the robots. Volumes of Inventor's Friends unlock further recipes as the protagonist gains levels. Scrap supplies material for basic equipment and stronger combinations. Weapons can also be combined with others of the same type to improve them, giving previously acquired equipment another use.

cards.heading: One robot on the battlefield
cards.text: Battles are engaged by contact with the enemy on a map. The player usually attacks first, unless the enemy has caught the player's side or from behind. Battling in the game takes place on a battlefield under a variation of the ATB system, in which the player must wait for a gauge to fill up before acting. Only one robot may fight at any time up against at most three enemies; the player can switch between robots at the cost of a turn (like in Pokémon). During the player's turn, none of the enemies will act, and the robot is free to move around the battlefield and attack with one of its weapons. After the robot acts, a gauge appears with the letters E (empty) and F (full) at either end. The gauge's depletion will depend on what action the player used. Until the gauge reaches F, all enemies take turns attacking.

main.title: Shining Force CD
main.subtitle: Four books of tactical battles
main.summary: Shining Force CD is Sonic! Software Planning's tactical role-playing game, first released for Mega-CD in Japan on 22 July 1994.

cards.heading: Four books of tactical battles
cards.text: Shining Force CD is Sonic! Software Planning's tactical role-playing game, first released for Mega-CD in Japan on 22 July 1994. Its first two books adapt Shining Force Gaiden and Gaiden II from Game Gear, followed by two new scenarios that continue their stories. The player leads a force through turn-based battles, choosing where individual characters move and which opponent or ally receives their next action. Short scenes connect the encounters, giving the campaign a concentrated rhythm of preparation, a battlefield problem and the consequences that lead into the next book.

cards.heading: The force between encounters
cards.text: The fighting follows the Gaiden games' tactical structure, with individual units moving across a map and acting when their turn arrives. Between battles, the player can save, promote characters, revive fallen companions and sometimes buy or sell equipment. These pauses keep the force ready without requiring a separate free-roaming town. A unit's development matters across successive encounters, so choosing how to use a weaker character also concerns the army's future. The next map draws on that preparation, asking the player to bring the available strengths together around another arrangement of enemies and terrain.

cards.heading: Carrying a party into another chapter
cards.text: Completing the first two books opens the third, while the fourth also requires a hidden item. Character statistics can carry into those later scenarios through a backup RAM cartridge, extending the value of the force already developed. The hardware's internal memory is insufficient to preserve all the necessary book data together, making the accessory relevant to that continuity. Motoaki Takenouchi composed the score. Shining Force CD uses the disc as a home for a linked campaign, expanding two portable adventures into a longer sequence whose later challenges depend on the party built earlier.

main.title: Pulseman
main.subtitle: Pulseman Reveals Game Freak Before Pokémon
main.summary: On July 22, 1994 Sega released Pulseman for Mega Drive in Japan, developed by Game Freak.

cards.heading: Pulseman Reveals Game Freak Before Pokémon
cards.text: On July 22, 1994 Sega released Pulseman for Mega Drive in Japan, developed by Game Freak. Directed by Ken Sugimori and made with figures who would become central to Pokémon, including Satoshi Tajiri and Junichi Masuda, the platformer builds its movement around electricity. Running fast enough lets the hero become a pulse and ricochet off surfaces, merging speed and puzzles.

cards.heading: Half human, half C-Life
cards.text: Pulseman is the child of computer engineer Doc Yoshiyama and C-Life, an artificial intelligence the scientist created. Unlike an ordinary digital being, he can survive outside a computer. His body can channel electricity as a weapon and use the Volteccer power for rapid transport.

cards.heading: The Galaxy Gang
cards.text: Unfortunately, living in the computer world for so long twisted Doc Yoshiyama's mind, corrupting his brainwaves and his body. Doc Yoshiyama emerged back into the human world, but twisted and changed into the evil Doc Waruyama. Using a system known as EUREKA, which allows for C-Life beings to manifest in the human world, Doc Waruyama establishes the Galaxy Gang, spreading a new wave of cyber-terrorism across the world. Pulseman must fight his own father and put an end to his gang for the sake of the free world.

cards.heading: Game Freak before Pokemon
cards.text: When first announced, the game was titled Spark. It was directed by Ken Sugimori. Much of the staff who worked on Pulseman would later work on the Pokémon series, including Sugimori, designer Satoshi Tajiri, artist Atsuko Nishida, and composer Junichi Masuda.

main.title: Policenauts
main.subtitle: A detective adventure directed by Hideo Kojima
main.summary: On July 29, 1994 Policenauts debuted on the PC-9821 and pushed Hideo Kojima toward another form of interactive direction.

cards.heading: Investigating a science-fiction mystery
cards.text: Policenauts debuted on the PC-9821 on July 29, 1994. Hideo Kojima's adventure combines investigation through dialogue, objects and inventory with occasional bursts of action. Buddy movies, police science fiction and animation shape its presentation. Players examine scenes and pursue conversations to advance the story, while later console versions expanded the animated sequences and added subtitles.

cards.heading: Investigating with a cursor
cards.text: Policenauts is a graphic adventure game with a point-and-click interface. It has also been called a visual novel and an interactive movie. The player moves a cursor freely across the screen to click on objects to examine them. During conversations, the player is given dialogue options to choose from. Once the right object in the scene has been examined or the dialogue options have been exhausted, the game progresses to the next scene in the story. In versions with cel animation, these scenes the player must examine are stills from the animated cinematics, so the game moves seamlessly between them and cutscenes. There are occasional action scenes where the player must fire a gun at enemies in a first-person perspective. The Sega Saturn version supports a light gun for these segments.

cards.heading: Giving the director control
cards.text: After Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake, Hideo Kojima developed a scripting engine to control when animations and music played without having to ask programmers to implement each change. He wrote and implemented Policenauts' text-based portion in 1990. At first it remained a technical project without the resources for full production; development ultimately lasted four years.

cards.heading: Why later versions added subtitles
cards.text: Policenauts was first released for the PC-9821 on July 29, 1994. Kojima received a letter from a hearing-impaired player after release, upset that modern games like Policenauts with its CD-ROM technology were replacing game text with actual speech. Kojima originally omitted subtitles to evoke a cinematic feel, but he added them for following versions to satisfy the players. The first port was for the 3DO Interactive Multiplayer and released on September 29, 1995. A short demo with a game glossary, artwork, and design documents was released on April 21, 1995, called the Pilot Disk. The 3DO version and subsequent console ports had a drop in display resolution, and used newly animated full motion video in contrast to the animated stills used in the PC version. The visuals were animated by Anime International Company using traditional cel animation techniques.

main.title: Monster Max
main.subtitle: Rare · Game Boy
main.summary: Monster Max is Rare's Game Boy isometric puzzle adventure about an aspiring rock star opposing King Krond's ban on music. Max enters the Mega Hero Academy, working through its floors and completing tasks that earn access to further rooms. The view makes blocks, platforms and the character's position central to understanding each problem. A small chamber can require several actions in a particular order, with movement around its objects providing the means of testing whether the apparent solution actually leaves a way to reach the next step.

cards.heading: A musician trains to challenge the king
cards.text: Monster Max is Rare's Game Boy isometric puzzle adventure about an aspiring rock star opposing King Krond's ban on music. Max enters the Mega Hero Academy, working through its floors and completing tasks that earn access to further rooms. The view makes blocks, platforms and the character's position central to understanding each problem. A small chamber can require several actions in a particular order, with movement around its objects providing the means of testing whether the apparent solution actually leaves a way to reach the next step.

cards.heading: Work out the order before committing
cards.text: Room objectives include collecting particular objects and dealing with enemies, while the academy's terminals explain the tasks ahead. The challenge depends on reading the arrangement and recognising which action needs to happen first. An object that looks easy to reach may still require another part of the room to be prepared. Gold earned through completed tasks pays for access to higher floors, linking each solved puzzle to the larger climb through the academy. The same small set of movements keeps acquiring another purpose as the rooms change.

cards.heading: The makers of Head over Heels return to isometric puzzles
cards.text: Jon Ritman handled design and programming, Bernie Drummond created the graphics and David Wise composed the music. Ritman and Drummond brought experience from Batman and Head over Heels, applying their interest in three-dimensional-looking rooms to the Game Boy. Titus released Monster Max in Europe in 1994 after development had finished much earlier. Its scale is expressed through a long sequence of carefully arranged spaces rather than an expansive view. The player becomes familiar with the little figure by repeatedly discovering what the next room allows him to do.

main.title: Dynamite Headdy
main.subtitle: A puppet whose head is his best weapon
main.summary: Treasure’s Dynamite Headdy turns a puppet theatre into a Mega Drive action game in 1994. Headdy fights an evil puppet ruler by throwing his own head, while the scenery behaves like part of a live performance. Backdrops, props and oversized enemies keep changing the scale of the action. The Japanese Mega Drive edition was released on August 5, 1994. Its theatrical setting does more than supply a colourful theme: it lets a platform, an enemy or a piece of scenery become the next surprise.

cards.heading: The stage fights back
cards.text: Treasure’s Dynamite Headdy turns a puppet theatre into a Mega Drive action game in 1994. Headdy fights an evil puppet ruler by throwing his own head, while the scenery behaves like part of a live performance. Backdrops, props and oversized enemies keep changing the scale of the action. The Japanese Mega Drive edition was released on August 5, 1994. Its theatrical setting does more than supply a colourful theme: it lets a platform, an enemy or a piece of scenery become the next surprise.

cards.heading: A different head for each occasion
cards.text: Seventeen power-up heads alter Headdy’s abilities, making the same basic throwing action serve different purposes. A new head can change his attacks or the way he moves, so recognising an item matters as much as reaching it. The manual even represents health through changes in the stage lighting rather than a conventional numerical display. Secret bonuses reward particular actions within scenes, inviting another look at apparently decorative details. The original music credits name Katsuhiko Suzuki, NON, Yasuko, Kouji and AKI as the composition team: the score accompanies the production’s constant shifts without reducing its world to a single musical mood.

main.title: Wild Guns
main.subtitle: A western with giant machines
main.summary: Wild Guns is Natsume’s Super Nintendo shooting-gallery game, combining a revenge story from the Wild West with robots and science-fiction machinery. Annie enlists the bounty hunter Clint after her family is killed, and either character can be controlled through the adventure. They move across the foreground while firing at enemies farther into the scene. A second player can join cooperatively. The resulting action combines the spectacle of an arcade shooting gallery with a vulnerable character whose position remains under the player’s control.

cards.heading: A western with giant machines
cards.text: Wild Guns is Natsume’s Super Nintendo shooting-gallery game, combining a revenge story from the Wild West with robots and science-fiction machinery. Annie enlists the bounty hunter Clint after her family is killed, and either character can be controlled through the adventure. They move across the foreground while firing at enemies farther into the scene. A second player can join cooperatively. The resulting action combines the spectacle of an arcade shooting gallery with a vulnerable character whose position remains under the player’s control.

cards.heading: Aim and stay alive
cards.text: The character and the target do not occupy the same depth. Enemies appear across the background while Annie or Clint must evade attacks in front, sidestepping and jumping as the fight develops. Watching only the reticle leaves the character exposed; watching only the character wastes opportunities to clear the scene. That division gives even a fixed viewpoint a demanding sense of movement. The player has to coordinate where shots are going with where the next incoming attack will arrive, often in the company of a cooperative partner.

cards.heading: Small scenes, large opponents
cards.text: Six levels organise their action into encounters that build toward larger enemies and bosses. Natsume’s small development team gives the western setting a distinctive mechanical scale, placing familiar frontier imagery beside exaggerated machines. The cooperative mode shares that screen with another player, while target practice provides a separate score competition. These modes use the same clear relationship between the foreground fighters and their distant targets. Wild Guns finds variety in what enters the scene and how its fire forces the characters to move.

main.title: The King of Fighters '94
main.subtitle: SNK brings its fighters together
main.summary: The King of Fighters '94 is SNK's crossover fighting game, first released for Neo Geo MVS on 25 August 1994.

cards.heading: SNK brings its fighters together
cards.text: The King of Fighters '94 is SNK's crossover fighting game, first released for Neo Geo MVS on 25 August 1994. It brings characters from Fatal Fury, Art of Fighting, Ikari Warriors and Psycho Soldier into a tournament alongside new fighters led by Kyo Kusanagi. Three-member teams replace the usual isolated contestant, giving the event a broader cast and another layer of preparation. The tournament's organiser, Rugal Bernstein, supplies the final threat. Its success established an annual series that would become one of SNK's central identities in the arcade.

cards.heading: Choosing the order of the team
cards.text: The player chooses one of eight fixed teams, then decides the order in which its members will fight. A defeated character gives way to the next teammate, while the winner remains with a small amount of health restored. The match ends when one side loses all three members. That continuity makes the opening fighter's performance matter to everybody following them. A strong first round can remove an opponent and leave another rival facing a weakened but still dangerous character, turning a succession of duels into one extended team contest.

cards.heading: Power with a moment of risk
cards.text: Four attack buttons distinguish light and strong punches and kicks. The power gauge grows through defensive exchanges and damage, and can also be charged manually, although doing so leaves the fighter exposed. Filling it strengthens attacks temporarily and enables a powerful special move. Teammates waiting at the edge can also assist under the appropriate conditions, making their presence more than decorative. The combination gives the crossover a shared structure: familiar characters bring their own techniques, while the gauge and team order make them part of the same tactical contest.
